questions.prompt: What does committing more often buy you, according to the practice of continuous integration?
choices: Errors found sooner, and less code to search when one appears
Fewer merge conflicts with no review
questions.explain: Frequent commits mean a failure points at a small change, instead of days of tangled work.

questions.prompt: Why does running tests on a runner settle a 'works on my machine' argument?
choices: The check runs the same way every time, on a machine nobody has been configuring
Runners use the same operating system as production
questions.explain: The value is repeatability: one definition of the check, run somewhere neutral.

questions.prompt: Which of these can a CI workflow reasonably include?
choices: Linters, type checks, tests, coverage, and security scans
questions.explain: Anything you could run yourself can run in the workflow, and its result reports on the pull request.

questions.prompt: What separates continuous delivery from continuous deployment?
choices: Deployment removes the human decision before production
questions.explain: Both produce something releasable. Deployment simply removes the button a person presses.

questions.prompt: A team wants to move from delivery to deployment. What has to be true first?
choices: Their checks must be trustworthy enough that a human reading the same green ticks adds nothing
They must remove all manual tests
questions.explain: The button is a safety net for checks you do not fully trust. Remove the doubt first, then the button.

questions.prompt: Why do the concepts transfer between Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI, and others?
choices: They all express events, jobs, steps, runners, artifacts, and environments under some name
They are built on the same engine
questions.explain: The vocabulary differs, the shape does not, which is what makes the knowledge portable in an interview.

choices: Every repository, up to a monthly limit
Public repositories on standard hosted runners, and self-hosted runners
questions.explain: Public repositories using standard GitHub-hosted runners are free, as are self-hosted runners.

questions.prompt: In a private repository, who is billed for the minutes a workflow uses?
choices: The person who triggered the run
The organisation that owns the runner
questions.explain: Anyone with write access can start a run, and the cost falls to the repository owner.

questions.prompt: You delete a large artifact halfway through the billing cycle. What happens to the bill?
choices: Future hourly charges stop, but storage already accrued still appears
Nothing changes until the next cycle
questions.explain: Storage accrues hourly. Deleting stops the accrual from that moment; it does not undo what accrued already.

questions.prompt: Why is a slow pipeline a cost problem as well as a waiting problem?
choices: Minutes are consumed on every run of every job, so the cost repeats on every pull request
GitHub charges extra for long jobs
questions.explain: The bill scales with how often the pipeline runs, which is why caching and filters save money and time together.
